# Samuddavāṇijajātaka (Ja 466)

**ID:** Ja 466  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Samuddavāṇijajātaka

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Samuddavāṇijajātaka* (Ja 466), translated into English as *The Sea-Merchants*, belongs to the Pali Jātaka collection. According to the traditional framing narrative, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana concerning Devadatta, after the latter had fallen into hell taking five hundred families with him [Fausböll 1887]. The opening verse of the text begins with the words *Kasanti vapanti te janā* [Fausböll 1887].

Charles Eliot highlights the story as evidence that maritime voyages and large-scale maritime migrations were familiar themes in ancient Indian society [Eliot 1921]. A verse from this Jātaka also finds a corresponding form in the Prakrit Dhammapada [Barua 1921].

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 4 (1887) — Pali title, incipit, and framing context regarding Devadatta and the five hundred families.
- [Eliot 1921] Charles Eliot, Hinduism and Buddhism: An Historical Sketch, Vol. 3 (1921) — Summary of the carpenter village migration by sea and discussion of ancient Indian seafaring.
- [Barua 1921] Benimadhab Barua, Prakrit Dhammapada (1921) — Narrative details regarding the carpenters' escape from creditors, landing on the island, and factional division; verse parallel in Prakrit Dhammapada.
